prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology and peptide identity of glucagon-like peptide-1 that made possible incretin-based therapy of type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: All six opening ballots rank B001 first, but I do not treat that unanimity as the argument. The scientific case is that it is a complete chain: proglucagon-derived peptide biology, the demonstration in humans that GLP-1 is a glucose-dependent incretin, identification and synthesis of the active GLP-1(7-36) form, and then receptor agonists with durable effects on glycaemia, body weight and now cardiovascular and renal outcomes. The mechanism is replicated across many independent laboratories and the clinical benefit is confirmed in large randomised trials, so the discovery is mature and, if anything, overdue. A single-achievement prize with Holst for physiology and secretion, Drucker for GLP-1 and GLP-2 biology and its translational logic, and Mojsov for identification and synthesis of the active peptide is the cleanest allocation that fits the three-person limit.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution. The three-person limit leaves out Knudsen, whose long-acting analogue chemistry is what made the drugs practical, and priority for identifying the active peptide is disputed, including contributions from the Habener group that are not in the credited names. A prize built on basic physiology risks being read as under-crediting the drug-development step that produced the clinical effect, while a prize that includes Knudsen would have to drop one of the three academic discoverers. If the committee cannot settle these credit questions, a different candidate with a cleaner allocation, such as B043, or a clearer therapeutic-modality case such as B045, may be easier to defend.

responses.point: Linnarsson ranks B012 third and B043 fourth, and for B045 names only June and Sadelain, treating Rosenberg and the original chimeric receptor concept as an attribution problem.
responses.response: I agree that B045 has a real attribution gap, since the first chimeric receptor concept is not in the credited names, and this is a main reason I keep it as an alternative and not as a second prize part. I would not go as far as preferring B012 to it. HPV vaccines are a major prevention achievement, but zur Hausen's prize already covered the viral aetiology and the VLP priority dispute is unresolved. I would put B045 ahead on conceptual novelty, as a new therapeutic modality.

responses.point: Svenningsson, speaking as a neurologist, argues that Knudsen's drug-development role is real but industrial and would be the first to be left out, and he ranks B014 (Benabid) and B012 above B043.
responses.response: I accept his ordering of credit within B001 and share his caution about paying for drug development, but I would state it more carefully. The prize cannot say that industrial work is lesser. The question is which three people made the decisive, identifiable steps, and for GLP-1 that is a closer call than the opening ballots imply. I also disagree on B043 versus B014. Mori and Walter give a two-person claim with little ambiguity, whereas for deep brain stimulation I would want to settle first how much of the credit belongs to the basal ganglia circuit work that guided target choice. A one-person prize would not resolve that.

responses.point: Sandberg puts B039 third and B003 fourth, and ranks B042 (cGAS-STING) fifth, praising their conceptual breadth while noting that B039 has crowded credit and that B042 is early clinically.
responses.response: I accept that optogenetics is among the most influential advances of the period, but I am more cautious than Sandberg. The credit is spread over six names with at least three strong claimants to exclude, and it is mainly a method, so I would not use it as a second part of a shared prize. On B042 I agree with his own reservation: the mechanism is clear, but pathway modulation has not yet shown clinical benefit, so I would wait. I agree with him that the 2002 prize makes B003 require a clearly distinct achievement, and that the Tsujimoto and Korsmeyer omission is a real problem.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius ranks B043 third and B003 fourth, argues that the UPR gives a clean two-person allocation, and notes that B004 was already given the Lasker award and may be late recognition.
responses.response: I agree about B043: the Mori and Walter pair has the cleanest attribution on the shortlist and I rank it highly on science alone. My difference is on B004. A prior Lasker award is not a reason to rank it lower, since it is not a Nobel criterion, and the clinical proof of principle for kinase-targeted therapy is as clear as for any shortlisted case. My reservation about B004 is the upstream BCR-ABL discoveries outside the credited names, not the length of time since the drug appeared. I therefore keep it as a serious alternative despite her ranking it seventh.

responses.point: El Manira ranks B040 (SMN2 splicing and nusinersen) third and notes that Knudsen would have to be omitted from B001, while ranking B045 second.
responses.response: I agree that B040 is a mechanistically clear success and a strong RNA-therapeutics case, and a two-person Krainer and Bennett allocation is coherent, but I rank it below B004 and B045 because the SMN1 gene discovery lies outside the credited names and the field is newer. On Knudsen, I read the same issue differently from him: the objection is not that she is minor but that the three-person limit forces a choice, and I would rather make that choice openly in the citation than mask it by widening the wording.

uncertainties: Whether the committee can agree on allocating credit for identifying the active GLP-1 peptide, given the Habener group contribution that is not among the credited names.
Whether a single-achievement prize is preferable to pairing GLP-1 with a second distinct achievement (for example B045 or B043) when the three-person limit would then force fewer names on B001.
Whether the omission of Knudsen is acceptable in a citation that must still convey the drug-development step.
My recollection of GLP-1 chronology rests on background knowledge and not on independent verification.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile for the shortlisted candidates: my own work on nuclear receptors and midbrain dopamine neurons is in a different field, and the profile lists no connection to any credited name on the shortlist. The profile does record past co-authorship with Svenningsson and, once, El Manira, which I note for transparency but do not regard as a conflict.
